questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: this course calls Order-to-Cash a ________, not a one-way transaction, because what happens at the end of one sale — a customer's payment history, an unresolved dispute — can affect how the next one is handled.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 draws this distinction deliberately: a purchase is a transaction that happens once and finishes, but Order-to-Cash is a cycle because the outcome of one sale (payment history, open disputes, risk tier) feeds directly into how the next sale is credit-checked and approved. Treating O2C as a straight line instead of a loop is called out as one of the most common mistakes a new consultant makes.

questions.prompt: Match each stage of the Order-to-Cash customer lifecycle to the role typically responsible for it, per lesson 2.
right: An accountant, working in Subledger Accounting and General Ledger
Order administration or inside sales, working in Order Management
A billing specialist, working in Receivables, usually through AutoInvoice
Credit and collections analysts, and sometimes a manager approving in AME
questions.explain: Order capture is owned by order administration or inside sales in Order Management. Order validation is owned by credit and collections analysts, sometimes with AME approval. Billing is owned by a billing specialist in Receivables, usually via AutoInvoice. Reconciliation is owned by an accountant working in Subledger Accounting and General Ledger — the six-stage lifecycle lesson 2 lays out before any single transaction is followed in detail.

questions.prompt: A warehouse worker ships a quantity that the sales order never authorized. Per lesson 2, why does this count as a real Order-to-Cash problem rather than just a shipping inconvenience?
options: Because most real O2C problems happen at the handoffs between stages and people, not inside any single screen — an unauthorized shipped quantity breaks the agreement between what Order Management decided and what Shipping actually did.
Because Shipping is not allowed to touch inventory without a signature from a General Ledger accountant first.
Because any shipped quantity automatically triggers a credit check hold, regardless of what the order authorized.
Because Order Management will silently cancel the entire order the moment a shipped quantity doesn't match.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 makes the point that every handoff between O2C stages is also a handoff between people, and most real problems happen exactly there — a warehouse shipping a quantity the order didn't authorize is its own named example. As a consultant, the useful first question is whose stage the transaction was in and what their screen shows, not which table a field lives in.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Order-to-Cash setup, per lesson 3.
options: Business unit, legal entity, chart of accounts, customer account/site, and Receivables transaction types are all setup objects O2C reuses directly from earlier courses.
Item and pricing setup, order orchestration/fulfillment rules, credit check rules, and shipping parameters are setup that's new to Order Management specifically.
Order Management maintains its own separate customer list, independent of the customer records used in Receivables.
A missing or misconfigured setup object, like a customer site with no active price list, is one of the most common causes of a stuck order.
Credit check and hold rules are reused directly from the Accounts Receivable course, with no new configuration needed for Order Management.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 splits setup into two groups: reused setup (business unit, legal entity, chart of accounts, customer account/site, transaction types, receipt classes) and setup that's new to Order Management (items/pricing, orchestration rules, credit check and hold rules, shipping parameters). Order Management reads the same customer records Receivables uses — it does not maintain a separate list. A missing setup object, like a site with no active price list, is named directly as a common root cause of a stuck order. Credit check rules are called out as new setup, not something carried over unchanged from Accounts Receivable.

questions.prompt: Put these five areas of Oracle Fusion in the order a single sales order touches them, per lesson 1.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 lays out the one-event-five-stops shape of O2C in this order: Order Management captures and validates the order, Inventory and Shipping physically fulfills it, Receivables turns the shipment into an invoice, Cash Management receives and matches the payment, and General Ledger — by way of Subledger Accounting — records the accounting impact of everything that happened before it.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a hold from an approval in Oracle Fusion Order Management, per lesson 8?
options: An approval is an automatic system stop triggered whenever a defined condition is met, such as a credit check failing, while a hold is instead a decision that gets routed to a person before an action is allowed to proceed.

A hold is an automatic system stop triggered when a defined condition is met, such as a credit check failing, while an approval is a decision routed to a person before an action is allowed to proceed.
Holds and approvals both require a person to manually review and release them before an order can proceed, differing only in which department handles each one.
A hold can only ever be applied to an entire order, never to a single line, while an approval always applies to just one line.
An approval is simply Oracle's term for any credit check, while a hold refers only to a price override needing a manager's sign-off.
A hold is permanent once applied and can never be released, while an approval can be reversed at any time by the person who originally requested it.
questions.explain: Lesson 8 defines the two terms precisely: a hold is an automatic stop the system applies itself when a condition like a credit check fails, while an approval is a request routed to a person — often through AME — before an action can proceed. Credit checks are named as the most common source of a hold specifically because the system checks the condition and applies the hold without anyone having to request anything.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A states the exact right definitions but swaps which word they belong to — it's a hold, not an approval, that's the automatic system stop, and an approval, not a hold, that's routed to a person for a decision. Getting the two terms backwards is precisely the mix-up lesson 8 draws the line on, and it reads as deceptively correct if you don't track which noun pairs with which definition.

questions.prompt: Suppose, before fulfillment begins, Harborview calls back and reduces SO-48217's quantity from 400 units to 350 units. The order's automatic volume discount rule fires at 300 units or more. What happens to the discount, and why, per lesson 9?
options: The 5% discount still applies, because 350 units still clears the 300-unit threshold — it just applies against a smaller base.
The discount is lost entirely, because any change to a submitted order's quantity cancels all previously applied discounts.
The discount increases to a higher tier, because reducing the quantity pushes the order into a different pricing agreement.
The order must go through a price override approval, because any quantity change requires re-approval of the discount.
questions.explain: Lesson 9 walks through exactly this hypothetical: because fulfillment hasn't started, the line quantity can simply be updated, and Order Management re-prices it against the same automatic discount rule. 350 units still clears the 300-unit volume threshold, so the 5% discount still applies — just against a smaller base of units, not against the original 400.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on a sales order header, the ________ site drives where the Receivables invoice is sent and which payment terms and tax rules apply, while the ship-to site drives which warehouse fulfills the order.
questions.explain: Lesson 5 separates the bill-to decision from the ship-to decision on purpose: the ship-to address drives which warehouse fulfills the order and how freight is calculated, while the bill-to site drives where the Receivables invoice is sent and which payment terms and tax rules apply — two independent addresses captured on the same order header.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about order pricing and discounts, per lesson 7.
options: An order line prices against a specific price list, determined by the customer, business unit, or a negotiated agreement.
An automatic discount applies whenever an order meets a defined condition, such as a quantity threshold, without anyone requesting it.
A price below the standard discount policy's floor typically requires no approval, since Order Management trusts every user's pricing judgment.
A negotiated agreement can override the standard price list entirely for a specific customer.
SO-48217's 5% discount required a manager's approval because it exceeded standard pricing policy.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 describes a price list as the starting point for an order line, adjusted by automatic discounts (system-applied when a condition like a quantity threshold is met), manual discounts, or negotiated agreements that override the standard price list entirely. A price below the policy floor is exactly the kind of override lesson 7 says typically needs approval — the opposite of needing none. SO-48217's 5% discount is a standard, pre-approved automatic rule, so it specifically did not need any override approval.

questions.prompt: Match each pricing or approval term to what it actually is, per lessons 7 and 8.
right: An automatic system stop applied when a condition, like a credit limit check, fails
A decision routed to a person, often through AME, before an action is allowed to proceed
A discount the system applies on its own whenever an order meets a defined condition
A change outside standard pricing rules that typically needs its own approval
questions.explain: An automatic discount is system-applied the moment a defined condition is met. A price override is a change outside the standard rules, which typically needs approval. A credit check hold is an automatic stop the system applies when a condition like a credit limit check fails. An approval is a decision routed to a person, often through AME, before the order can proceed — four related but distinct mechanisms from lessons 7 and 8.

questions.prompt: What specifically triggers inventory depletion for a shipped order line, per lesson 12?
options: Shipping confirmation — the action that tells Oracle Fusion the staged goods actually left the warehouse.
Submitting the sales order, since that's when inventory is reserved against the order.
Picking the items from their storage location, since that's when they physically leave the shelf.
Running AutoInvoice, since that's when the system recognizes the sale financially.
questions.explain: Lesson 12 is explicit that confirming a shipment is what finalizes the actual shipped quantity and triggers inventory depletion — goods are removed from on-hand inventory because they are no longer physically there. Picking stages goods for packing, but it's ship confirmation, not picking, submission, or AutoInvoice, that actually depletes inventory and starts Interface Trip Stop.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: released order lines are normally grouped into a pick ________ — a batch of work released to the warehouse floor together, often based on shared criteria like ship date or carrier.
questions.explain: Lesson 11 introduces the pick wave as the way a warehouse plans efficient picking runs instead of chasing one released line at a time, grouping lines released together by shared criteria such as ship date, carrier, or shipping dock.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about short picks, shipping, and returns, per Chapter 3.
options: A short pick happens when fewer units are actually available to pick than the order line requested.
Oracle Fusion will automatically substitute a different warehouse that has stock if the originally specified ship-from organization is short.
After a line has shipped, reducing its quantity requires a return rather than a simple edit.
An RMA is a return order that references the original sales order, rather than a disconnected, brand-new transaction.
Ship confirmation can be safely skipped for a shipment that definitely occurred, since inventory updates automatically either way.
questions.explain: A short pick is defined in lesson 11 as fewer units available than requested. Lesson 10 is explicit that Oracle Fusion will not silently substitute a different warehouse with stock — a shortage has to be addressed directly. Lesson 9 establishes that quantity reductions after shipping require a return, and lesson 13 defines an RMA as a return order referencing the original sales order. Lesson 12 warns that a shipment that leaves the dock without ship confirmation is a real, recurring problem precisely because inventory does NOT update on its own without that step.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the RMA process in the correct order, per lesson 13.
items: Request — an RMA is created referencing the original sales order
Authorization — the RMA is approved, generating a receiving record for the inbound units
Receipt — the returned units physically arrive and are recorded against the RMA
Inspection — a quality check decides whether the units can be resold, repaired, or must be scrapped
Billing resolution — the RMA line moves to "awaiting billing," enabling a credit memo
questions.explain: Lesson 13 walks through the RMA process in exactly this order: request a return referencing the original order, authorize it so the warehouse knows units are inbound, receive the units physically, inspect them to decide their disposition, and only then move to billing resolution, which is what makes a credit memo possible.

questions.prompt: A shipment physically leaves the warehouse dock, but the ship confirmation step in Oracle Fusion is never performed because of a process gap. What is the most likely downstream consequence, per lesson 12?
options: The order sits indefinitely in an "awaiting shipping" status, inventory still looks on-hand when it isn't, and the customer never gets billed for goods they already received.
Nothing — Interface Trip Stop runs automatically on a timer regardless of whether ship confirmation happened.
The order is automatically cancelled once the system detects the goods are missing from inventory counts.
AutoInvoice creates the invoice anyway, using the originally planned quantity instead of the confirmed one.
questions.explain: Lesson 12 names this exact scenario as a common, real-world failure point: without ship confirmation, a line stays stuck awaiting shipping, inventory still looks on-hand when it physically isn't, and the customer never gets billed — because Interface Trip Stop, inventory depletion, and invoicing eligibility all depend on ship confirmation actually having run.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes an applied credit memo from an on-account credit, per lesson 17?
options: The real difference is which module creates the record — applied credit memos come from Order Management, while on-account credits come from Receivables.
An on-account credit can only be issued for returned goods that failed inspection, while an applied credit memo covers every other kind of billing adjustment.

An on-account credit references a specific invoice and immediately reduces that invoice's open balance, while an applied credit memo isn't tied to any invoice at all and just sits as an available balance until someone eventually applies it.

An applied credit memo references a specific invoice and immediately reduces that invoice's open balance, while an on-account credit isn't tied to a specific invoice and sits as an available balance until someone applies it.
Both types of credit are applied automatically to the customer's single oldest open invoice, regardless of which transaction actually generated the credit.
An applied credit memo increases the customer's open balance, while an on-account credit decreases it the moment it's created.
questions.explain: Lesson 17 is explicit: a credit memo generated with a direct reference back to an original invoice is an applied credit memo, reducing that invoice's open balance immediately, while an on-account credit isn't tied to a specific invoice and instead sits as an available balance until someone applies it later. SO-48217's return-driven credit memo is applied for exactly this reason — it traces back through the RMA to a specific invoice.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C states the right pair of definitions but swaps which term each one belongs to — it's the applied credit memo, not the on-account credit, that ties to a specific invoice and reduces it right away; the on-account credit is the one that sits unapplied until someone matches it later. That single swap is the error, and it reads as correct unless you carefully track which noun goes with which behavior.

questions.prompt: AutoInvoice runs against a staged shipment line, and the line is rejected because the customer's bill-to site has no remit-to address assigned. What does this rejection actually mean, per lesson 16?
options: The record stays safely in the Receivables interface tables, unconverted, until the remit-to address is added and AutoInvoice is run again.
The shipment data is permanently lost and the line has to be re-shipped from the warehouse to generate a new invoice.
Receivables automatically assigns a default remit-to address so the invoice can still be created on this same run.
The order itself gets cancelled, since AutoInvoice treats a rejection the same way Order Management treats a credit check failure.
questions.explain: Lesson 16 is clear that a rejected or errored record stays in the interface tables — nothing is lost — and simply doesn't become a real transaction until it's corrected. The fix, using Manage AutoInvoice Lines, is to assign the missing remit-to address and resubmit AutoInvoice, exactly what happens to SO-48217's line in that lesson, with no re-shipment and no order cancellation involved.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: shipment data reaches Receivables in two steps — the Invoicing Integration workflow activity stages the data in the Receivables interface tables, and ________ then validates it and creates the real Receivables transaction.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 separates the handoff into two distinct steps run by two different parts of the system: Invoicing Integration packages and writes shipment data to the Receivables interface tables, and AutoInvoice is the Receivables program that reads, validates, and converts qualifying staged rows into real transactions.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how an Order-to-Cash invoice's fields are determined, per lesson 14.
options: The bill-to customer and site on the invoice come from the order header's bill-to, not a value Receivables decides independently.
Quantity invoiced comes from the confirmed shipped quantity, not necessarily the originally ordered quantity.
Invoice date and GL date always have to be the same value, by Oracle Fusion's design.
Unit price on the invoice reflects the order line's negotiated price, after any discount.
A billing clerk manually re-keys every invoice line from scratch, independent of what Order Management and Shipping already captured.
questions.explain: Lesson 14's field mapping table shows bill-to, quantity invoiced, and unit price all carrying forward from the order header and the confirmed shipment, not re-decided or re-typed by Receivables. Invoice (transaction) date and GL date are explicitly called out as usually matching but not required to — a shipment near month-end invoiced the next day is the example given for when they diverge. The entire point of lesson 14 is that none of this is re-typed by a billing clerk; it's carried forward automatically from decisions already made in Order Management and Shipping.

questions.prompt: A different order ships and invoices 600 units at a net discounted price of $42.50 per unit. 15 of those units are later returned and fail inspection. Following the same method lesson 17 used for SO-48217's credit memo, what should the resulting credit memo amount be, and at what unit price?
options: $637.50, calculated as 15 units × $42.50 — the same net discounted price the units were originally billed at.
$637.50, but only after first recalculating a brand-new list price for just the 15 returned units.
$25,500.00, calculated as 600 units × $42.50, crediting the entire original invoice regardless of how many units were returned.
$637.50, calculated using the item's undiscounted list price rather than the discounted price actually billed.
questions.explain: Lesson 17 calculates SO-48217's credit the same way: the returned units are credited at the same net, already-discounted unit price they were originally billed at, not the list price and not a newly recalculated price. 15 units × $42.50 = $637.50 — crediting exactly what the customer was charged for those specific units, no more and no less.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Receivables tracks how long an open invoice has been outstanding relative to its due date through ________ buckets, such as current, 1–30 days past due, and 31–60 days past due.
questions.explain: Lesson 18 introduces aging as the mechanism collections teams use to prioritize follow-up on open invoices, tracked through buckets like current, 1–30 days past due, and 31–60 days past due, relative to each invoice's due date.

questions.prompt: A customer's lockbox remittance references an invoice number that doesn't actually exist in Receivables — likely a typo. What happens to that customer's payment, per lesson 19?
options: The receipt is still created, recording that the cash arrived, but it's left unapplied, on account, for a cash applications specialist to match manually.
Lockbox processing rejects the payment outright and returns it to the customer's bank.
The payment is automatically applied to the customer's single oldest open invoice, regardless of what was referenced.
The receipt fails to create at all, since lockbox requires a valid invoice number to record any cash.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 is explicit that when remittance data doesn't match an open invoice cleanly, the receipt still gets created — the cash is recorded — but it generates recommended matches for a cash applications specialist to review and apply manually, rather than failing outright. This is called a routine, expected part of a collections team's daily work, not a sign something is broken.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Subledger Accounting entries an invoice, credit memo, and cash receipt generate, per lesson 20.
options: A standard invoice debits Receivable and credits Revenue for the invoiced amount.
A credit memo reverses part of the original entry, debiting Revenue and crediting Receivable.
Applying a cash receipt against an invoice debits Cash and credits Receivable, without touching Revenue again.
These journal entries are typed by hand by a Subledger Accounting user for every transaction.
A cash receipt's journal entry recognizes additional revenue on top of what the invoice already recognized.
questions.explain: Lesson 20 walks through all three entries exactly this way: the invoice debits Receivable and credits Revenue; the credit memo reverses part of that, debiting Revenue and crediting Receivable; and the cash receipt replaces the receivable with cash — Dr Cash, Cr Receivable — without touching Revenue again, since revenue was already recognized at invoicing. The whole point of the lesson is that Subledger Accounting's rule sets generate these entries automatically; no one types debits and credits by hand.

questions.prompt: Put these stages in the order accounting for an invoice actually moves from a business event to a posted General Ledger balance, per lessons 20 and 21.
items: A Receivables event, like an invoice, generates draft accounting from Subledger Accounting's journal entry rule sets
Create Accounting finalizes the draft into complete, balanced subledger journal entries
The finalized subledger entries transfer into General Ledger as journal entries
The transferred entries post, becoming part of the GL's balances for the period
questions.explain: Lesson 20 establishes that a Receivables event first generates draft accounting from SLA's rule sets. Lesson 21 then walks through Create Accounting's two stages: finalizing that draft into complete subledger journal entries, then transferring those finalized entries into GL and posting them so they become part of the period's GL balances — only final accounting, not draft, is ever eligible to transfer and post.

questions.prompt: Match each SO-48217 accounting event to the journal entry it generated, per lesson 20.
questions.explain: The invoice debits Receivable and credits Revenue for the full invoiced amount. The credit memo reverses part of that entry, debiting Revenue and crediting Receivable for the credited amount. The cash receipt replaces the remaining receivable with cash, debiting Cash and crediting Receivable, without touching Revenue — exactly the three entries lesson 20 walks through for SO-48217.

questions.prompt: While reconciling an order per lesson 22's framework, a consultant finds that the amount invoiced doesn't match the amount actually shipped. What does this specifically indicate, and what should the consultant check next?
options: The break is specifically at the shipment-to-invoice checkpoint, so the consultant should compare the confirmed shipped quantity and price against what was staged for AutoInvoice, rather than re-checking every other checkpoint from scratch.
The entire O2C cycle has failed, and every checkpoint from order to GL needs to be re-verified from the very beginning.
This is expected and requires no further investigation, since invoice and shipment amounts are allowed to differ freely.
The problem must be in the General Ledger posting, since that's always the last place a reconciliation discrepancy originates.
questions.explain: Lesson 22's whole point is that reconciliation is a chain of individually verifiable, neighbor-to-neighbor checkpoints — order to shipment, shipment to invoice, invoice to credit memo, invoice to receipt, subledger to GL — and when something doesn't tie out, the break is always at one specific checkpoint, not everywhere at once. A mismatch between shipped and invoiced amounts points specifically at the shipment-to-invoice handoff, not at every stage of the cycle.

questions.prompt: A customer orders 500 units; due to a cycle-count discrepancy, the warehouse can only pick and ship 460. What quantity does Oracle Fusion actually invoice, per lesson 24's short-shipment scenario?
options: 460 units — Oracle Fusion invoices what actually shipped, not what was originally ordered.
500 units, since the invoice always reflects the original order quantity regardless of what shipped.
480 units, splitting the difference between what was ordered and what shipped.
0 units, since a short shipment blocks invoicing entirely until the full quantity ships.
questions.explain: Lesson 24's short-shipment scenario states this directly: the line's actual shipped quantity becomes what gets invoiced, because Oracle Fusion invoices what shipped, not what was originally ordered. The remaining 40 units either back-order on the same line or require a separate decision from the customer.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the exception scenarios in lesson 24.
options: A price override beyond standard policy requires a true approval from someone with the right authority, unlike a credit check hold the system applies on its own.
A disputed invoice should be resolved by writing off the balance immediately, without comparing it back to the shipment.
A duplicate payment should never simply be deleted, since it represents real cash that has to be accounted for somewhere.
A short shipment's unshipped remainder either back-orders on the same line or requires a separate decision from the customer.
A disputed invoice that turns out to match its shipment exactly should still be credited, to keep the customer satisfied.
questions.explain: Scenario 2 distinguishes a true approval (needed for a policy-exceeding price override) from an automatic hold. Scenario 4 is explicit that a duplicate payment is never simply deleted, since it's real cash that has to be accounted for as an on-account credit or a refund. Scenario 1 states the short-shipment remainder back-orders or requires a customer decision. Scenario 3 is clear that a disputed invoice starts an investigation comparing it to its source shipment before anything is credited — and if the shipment and invoice genuinely agree, the dispute is resolved by sharing that evidence, not by crediting a balance that was actually correct.

questions.prompt: Put these five questions from lesson 25's troubleshooting checklist in the order they should be worked through for a stuck O2C transaction.
items: What stage is this transaction actually in?
Did the last expected event actually complete?
Is there a hold or a rejection sitting in the way?
Do the amounts actually agree at the nearest checkpoint?
Is the setup underneath this transaction actually complete?
questions.explain: Lesson 25's checklist runs in this order because each question narrows where the problem can live: first identify the stage, then confirm the last expected event completed, then check for a hold or rejection, then verify amounts agree at the nearest checkpoint, and finally rule out a setup gap — which is often the real cause hiding behind what looks like a shipping or billing problem.

questions.prompt: A line shipped three days ago but has generated no Receivables transaction. Manage AutoInvoice Lines shows a rejected record because the customer's item was never assigned to the price list this order uses. Per lesson 25's practice case, what kind of problem is this actually, and what's the fix?
options: It's a setup gap wearing a transaction's clothing — the fix is adding the missing price list assignment, then resubmitting AutoInvoice, not re-shipping anything.
It's a shipment problem — the warehouse needs to re-pick and re-ship the line before it can ever invoice.
It's a credit check problem — a credit analyst needs to release a hold before AutoInvoice can run again.
It's a cash application problem — a receipt needs to be manually matched to this line before it can invoice.
questions.explain: Lesson 25's first practice case walks through exactly this checklist: the line's status confirms it did ship, so the problem isn't fulfillment; Manage AutoInvoice Lines shows the real cause is a missing price list assignment for that customer's item — a setup gap, not a shipment problem. The fix is adding the missing price list assignment and resubmitting AutoInvoice, exactly the lesson's point that setup gaps often disguise themselves as something else.
